title: Is jazz better today than in the late twenties?
summary: Lovett and Goodwin say playing is better now because musicians study tone and theory more, as Parker did; Smith notes more models to hear.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You know, the problems in music that are always with us but the question that they ask is when were they most common, such as, intonation, swing, blend, tempo, poor reading, poor knowledge of changes as such, the bridges, the channels? Were these problems more common in the old days or are they very common today? What do you say, Baby?
I think you should mention that again, I didn't understand it all, I didn't understand that part.
Well, let me put it another way.
Would you say the quality of jazz music as it's played today is better or worse than it was in the late '20s and early '30s?
I think with the intonation and the

quality of the musicians that have had the chance of studying jazz music, more and everything, I think if you ask me, it's better. I'll have to digress some to the late '20s and the early '30s to where, I don't know, it seemed like music for jazz musicians, all of them didn't read good and they didn't work on their tones, they didn't practice tones; that is, whole notes to develop their tone and everything like the musician of today does.

I think they work a little harder at it now and I think they do a better job as to playing jazz. Now this is not to take anything away from guys like Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter. They were great during that time because the reason they were great, they were students of the music game. They put a lot of time into studying music, which made them top musicians and to this day Benny Carter is still a top musician.

He can take his place alongside with anybody when it comes to jazz music and I think this is what we're faced with now today. The music as it is played now is played by musicians who have had a much better schooling than the musicians back in the late '20s and the early '30s. I think this is where the turnover came where the guys began to think about, 'Well, I should study and not just go on what I've got, talent alone. I should try to develop this talent even greater'.

This even goes into the thing where Charlie Parker came along in the late '30s. I think that to me he was a genius of a musician but, however, he applied himself to music more and I think this is what made him so great and I think today the musicians that are coming along are going to be great because I think they study more; that is, for the most part.

And Crook, wouldn't you say that today and every year there are more and more great musicians to emulate, to copy, to listen to? The early day musicians didn't have too many people to listen to and learn from. Now today there are literally thousands of great jazz musicians that can be heard by the young people coming up, which wasn't true 40 years ago. You only had a handful to listen to, so it's a growing -- it's a snowballing effect which I think is tremendous. Baby, did you have anything more to say on this or should we go to the next question?
